rlch-01-c1.quote: another god, whom they call the heavenly Father, has no power in this world but does in the age to come
rlch-01-c1.claim: describes two principles: a good heavenly Father who rules the world to come and an evil maker who rules this one

rlch-01-c1.quote: This view, first argued in Frederick Conybeare's edition of the Key of Truth, was most convincingly detailed by Nina Garsoïan.
rlch-01-c1.claim: argued from Armenian sources that the early Paulicians were adoptionists, who saw Jesus as a man adopted as God's Son

rlch-01-c2.text: Bernard Hamilton (2017). Cathar Links with the Balkans and Byzantium. Cathars in Question, ed. Antonio Sennis (Boydell & Brewer / York Medieval Press).
rlch-01-c2.quote: In the days of the good Christian Tsar Peter [927–69], there was a priest [pop] called Bogomil.
rlch-01-c2.claim: In 10th-century Bulgaria, during the reign of Tsar Peter I (927 to 969), a priest called Bogomil began to preach.
